title: Who Is Fit to Lead?

theme: Socrates tests military experience against preparation, cooperation, and judgment

reading.title: Ὁ Νικομαχίδης καὶ ὁ Σωκράτης
reading.audioPlaceholder: Reading audio has not yet been recorded.
introduction: We pause the expedition for a separate scene in Athens. Nicomachides returns from the elections, disappointed that Antisthenes has been chosen general. Socrates questions what makes someone capable of leading.

Source: Xenophon, Memorabilia 3.4.1–12, with a short comparison to 3.1.1–7 on preparation. This present-tense dialogue simplifies and compresses Xenophon’s argument; its wording and connecting questions are adapted. Xenophon is not inserted as a witness. The elected Antisthenes is not identified here with the Socratic philosopher of the same name.

Blue glosses support irregular verbs, infinitives, and advanced forms. The lesson teaches new noun systems and question/indefinite words; military knowledge is a topic for discussion, not a demand that scars or wealth alone prove competence.

paragraphs.greek: Ἐν Ἀθήναις ὁ Νικομαχίδης ἀπὸ τῶν ἀρχαιρεσιῶν ἔρχεται. ὁ Σωκράτης αὐτὸν ὁρᾷ καὶ ἐρωτᾷ· «τίς στρατηγός ἐστιν; τί λέγουσιν οἱ πολῖται;»
Ὁ Νικομαχίδης λέγει· «ὁ Ἀντισθένης στρατηγός ἐστιν. ἐγὼ δὲ τῶν στρατιωτικῶν ἔργων ἐμπειρίαν ἔχω. πολλὰ τραύματα ἐν τῷ σώματι ἔχω.» καὶ τὰ τραύματα τῷ Σωκράτει δεικνύει.
«Ὁ δὲ Ἀντισθένης», λέγει, «χρήματα συλλέγει. ἆρα ἔμπορός τις ἱκανός ἐστιν ἄρχειν στρατιωτῶν;» ὁ Σωκράτης ἀποκρίνεται· «ὁ στρατηγὸς καὶ τροφὴν καὶ χρήματα παρασκευάζει.»

gloss.english: to command soldiers; infinitive plus genitive

paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Σωκράτης πάλιν ἐρωτᾷ· «τίς τοὺς χοροὺς καλῶς παρασκευάζει; ὁ Ἀντισθένης τοὺς ἐμπείρους ζητεῖ καὶ τοῖς ἐμπείροις τὰ ἔργα δίδωσιν.» ὁ Νικομαχίδης λέγει· «ἀλλὰ χορός τις οὐ στρατός ἐστιν.»
«Τίνος ἔργον», ὁ Σωκράτης λέγει, «τοὺς ἱκανοὺς ἄνδρας ζητεῖν καὶ τὰ χρήσιμα παρασκευάζειν; ὁ σώφρων ἄρχων οὐ μόνος πάντα πράττει. τοὺς ἀγαθοὺς βοηθοὺς αἱρεῖται.»

gloss.english: capable men; irregular noun form, glossed
the prudent leader; ἄρχων is used here as a noun

paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Νικομαχίδης ἀκούει. ὁ δὲ Σωκράτης λέγει· «ὁ τοῦ οἴκου φύλαξ καὶ ὁ τοῦ στρατοῦ ἄρχων τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐπιμελοῦνται. καὶ φίλους ζητοῦσι καὶ τὰ χρήματα φυλάττουσιν. οὐ μόνον πόνος, ἀλλὰ καὶ γνώμη χρήσιμός ἐστιν.»

gloss.english: care for people; genitive after care
useful; accent added before enclitic ἐστιν

paragraphs.greek: Ἕτερος λόγος τοῦ Σωκράτους καὶ περὶ παρασκευῆς ἐστιν. ὁ στρατηγὸς τὴν τροφὴν καὶ τὰ ὅπλα παρασκευάζει, τοὺς στρατιώτας τάττει καὶ τὴν ὁδὸν σκοπεῖ. οὐκ ἀρκεῖ μόνον τὴν τάξιν γιγνώσκειν.

gloss.english: it is not enough; impersonal use

paragraphs.greek: Νῦν πάλιν τὴν τοῦ Κύρου στρατιὰν σκοποῦμεν. ὁ ἡγεμὼν τοῖς στρατιώταις ὁδὸν δείκνυσιν· ὁ δὲ σώφρων στρατηγὸς τῶν στρατιωτῶν ἐπιμελεῖται. τίνος ἡ στρατιὰ χρῄζει; τίς ἱκανός ἐστιν ἄρχειν;

gloss.english: what does the army need?; χρῄζω takes genitive

reading.translation:
In Athens Nicomachides comes from the elections. Socrates sees him and asks: “Who is general? What do the citizens say?”

Nicomachides says: “Antisthenes is general. But I have experience of military work. I have many wounds on my body.” And he shows the wounds to Socrates.

“Antisthenes,” he says, “collects money. Is some merchant capable of commanding soldiers?” Socrates replies: “A general also provides food and money.”

Socrates asks again: “Who prepares the choruses well? Antisthenes seeks experienced people and assigns the tasks to them.” Nicomachides says: “But a chorus is not an army.”

“Whose task,” Socrates says, “is it to seek capable men and provide what is useful? The prudent leader does not do everything alone. He chooses good helpers.”

Nicomachides listens. Socrates says: “The guardian of a household and the leader of an army care for people. They both seek friends and protect resources. Not only effort, but also judgment is useful.”

Another account of Socrates also concerns preparation. The general provides food and weapons, organizes the soldiers, and examines the route. It is not enough to know only the formation.

Now we examine Cyrus’s army again. A guide shows the soldiers a route; a prudent general cares for the soldiers. What does the army need? Who is capable of leading?

wordStudy.label: Word Study — Experience and Practical Judgment

blocks.title: Words in the Reading
body: ἡγεμών is a guide or leader; ἄρχων can function as a noun meaning ruler or person in charge. In this lesson ἄρχων is a glossed noun. Its participial origin is not yet an assessed active-participle pattern.

ἐμπειρία is experience and ἔμπειρος describes an experienced person. γνώμη adds judgment; παρασκευή adds preparation. The argument asks how these abilities work together rather than replacing skill with money.

The question τίς; asks “who?” while enclitic τις supplies “someone” or “a certain.” Learn the accent and the context together: τίς στρατηγός ἐστιν; asks an identity; στρατηγός τις describes an unspecified general.

grammar.intro: Third-declension nasal, labial, and liquid stems; σώφρων; τίς and τις. Work through each section, use its checks and topic practice, then complete the grammar exercises. Reading-only forms remain supported by glosses.
objectives: Decline nasal, labial, and liquid noun models.
Explain ν + σ loss, labial + σ → ψ, and retained liquid stems.
Use σώφρων with masculine, feminine, and neuter nouns.
Ask who, what, whose, and to whom with accented τίς, τί.
Distinguish enclitic indefinite τις, τι from interrogative forms.

sections.title: 1. Nasal Stems
body: A nasal stem ends in ν. The genitive ἡγεμόνος reveals ἡγεμον-. Its nominative ἡγεμών uses a lengthened vowel without adding -ς. ποιμήν similarly has ποιμεν- in ποιμένος.

Add the consonant-declension endings to the stem: ἡγεμόν-α, ἡγεμόν-ες, ἡγεμόν-ων. In the dative plural ν drops before σ: ἡγεμον-σι becomes ἡγεμόσι. Learn the nominative and genitive together because a nominative alone can conceal the stem vowel.
The case still determines the job in the sentence. ὁ ἡγεμών is the subject; τὸν ἡγεμόνα is a direct object. The stem pattern is a new form of the same case system.

sections.title: 2. Labial and Liquid Stems
body: Labials π, β, φ combine with σ as ψ. The model Κύκλωψ has stem Κυκλωπ-, shown by Κύκλωπος. Its dative plural is Κύκλωψι. This is parallel to velar κ + σ → ξ from Lesson 13.

Liquid stems end in λ or ρ. ῥήτωρ has stem ῥητορ-, visible in ῥήτορος. It has no nominative -ς and has a lengthened nominative vowel; its dative plural ῥήτορσι retains ρ. Not every ρ-stem behaves exactly alike; Lesson 16 teaches family-noun alternations.

These models support case reading without forcing Cyclopes into the expedition. Κύκλωψ is a supplementary morphology example, not a character in our historical narrative. The article supplies the masculine gender of both models.

examples.greek: ὁ Κύκλωψ ἐν τῷ μύθῳ ἐστίν.
examples.english: The Cyclops is in the myth.

checks.prompt: How does a labial combine with σ?
checks.answer: π, β, or φ plus σ is written ψ.

sections.title: 3. The Adjective σώφρων
body: σώφρων means prudent or self-controlled. It has two nominative singular forms: σώφρων for masculine and feminine, σῶφρον for neuter. The genitive σώφρονος reveals σωφρον-.

The adjective agrees with its noun in gender, number, and case even when the masculine and feminine share a form. ὁ σώφρων στρατηγός and ἡ σώφρων γυνή both have σώφρων, but their articles and nouns have different gender.

A nasal stem loses ν before dative plural σ: σώφροσι. Neuter nominative and accusative match, σῶφρον in singular and σώφρονα in plural. Do not attach first/second-declension -ος, -η, -ον to this adjective.

checks.prompt: Which form agrees with neuter singular πρᾶγμα?

sections.title: 4. Asking Who and What
body: Accented τίς asks “who?” and τί asks “what?” They can be pronouns or adjectives: τίς ἄρχει; “who leads?”; τίς στρατηγὸς ἄρχει; “which general leads?” In direct questions τίς is masculine/feminine and τί is neuter.

Decline the question word for its function. τίνος means whose/of whom; τίνι means to whom; τίνα means whom (masculine/feminine direct object). Plural forms include τίνες, τίνων, τίσι(ν), and τίνας; neuter plural is τίνα.

The acute of interrogative τίς/τί remains acute, even before another word where an ordinary final acute might become grave. Use the form and the sentence role together: τίς asks the subject; τίνα asks an object.

examples.english: To whom do you bring food?

checks.prompt: Is τίς a pronoun in τίς ἄρχει;?
checks.answer: Yes; it stands alone as the subject.

sections.title: 5. Someone and Something
body: Enclitic τις means someone or a certain person; τι means something. As an adjective στρατηγός τις is “a certain general.” It does not ask a question. Unlike τίς, indefinite τις ordinarily has no written accent of its own.

The forms follow the same basic case endings: τινός, τινί, τινά; plural τινές, τινῶν, τισί(ν), τινάς. Enclitics lean on the preceding word for accent; two-syllable forms can keep or receive an accent under the normal enclitic rules. Accent alone is not a license to ignore context.

Notice ἔμπορός τις: the preceding word receives an additional acute because of the enclitic. This is different from τίς ἔμπορος; “which merchant?” A question can contain an indefinite: ἆρα ἔμπορός τις ἱκανός ἐστιν; asks whether some merchant is capable, not which merchant it is.

checks.prompt: Does τις necessarily ask a question?
checks.answer: No. It refers to an unspecified person or thing.

summary.title: Grammar Summary
items: Nasal ν drops before -σι; labials combine with σ as ψ; ρ remains in ῥήτορσι.
σώφρων serves masculine/feminine; σῶφρον is neuter; all forms agree with their nouns.
Accented τίς, τί asks a question; case identifies the role being questioned.
Enclitic τις, τι leaves a person or thing unspecified and can affect the preceding word’s accent.

sections.title: A disappointed candidate
body: Memorabilia 3.4 opens with Nicomachides returning from elections. He displays old wounds and points to his military service while complaining about the choice of Antisthenes. Xenophon uses this disagreement to examine what voters and candidates might count as qualifications. The passage does not tell us that visible scars are irrelevant; it questions whether they settle the whole issue.

Antisthenes here is the elected general discussed by Nicomachides and Socrates. A shared name does not establish that he is the Socratic philosopher known from other sources. The adaptation keeps the identification limited. It also keeps this scene in Athens, separate from the expedition, without claiming Xenophon heard the exchange himself.

sections.title: Why a chorus enters the argument
body: Nicomachides contrasts organizing a chorus with organizing troops. Socrates observes that Antisthenes has selected skilled specialists and successfully managed performances. The civic chorus is not a military unit, but both activities involve assigning work, securing resources, and directing people toward a shared result. In the passage, Antisthenes’s experience as a chorēgos supplies the comparison.

The analogy has limits that Nicomachides presses: actual fighting differs from performance. Socrates responds by considering practical preparation and readiness. We should evaluate this as an argument about transferable abilities, not a claim that theatrical success automatically certifies tactical expertise. The question for Cyrus’s army is which useful abilities it needs together.

sections.title: Preparation and the people being led
body: Memorabilia 3.1 criticizes instruction that reduces generalship to arranging formations. The discussion includes equipment, supplies, persistence, and the qualities needed to lead. Our short companion paragraph retains that breadth. Preparation is material work as well as a mental attitude; an army cannot survive on a confident speech alone.

Memorabilia 3.4 also compares household management and public leadership in their dealings with people. Choosing competent helpers and obtaining cooperation matter. The comparison raises an ethical question: how should a leader treat the people whose work makes success possible? It does not give us license to erase differences between a household, a city, and an army.

questions.answer: To support his claim that military experience qualifies him.

questions.prompt: Who is Antisthenes in this passage?
questions.answer: The elected general; the text used here does not establish that he is the Socratic philosopher.
It supplies an analogy for choosing skilled helpers and providing resources.
Organizing a performance is different from fighting a battle.

questions.prompt: What does preparation include beyond formation?
questions.answer: Supplies, equipment, skilled people, and readiness to act.

questions.prompt: How might the comparison apply to Cyrus’s army?
questions.answer: The army needs practical competence and care for people as well as military experience.
